learningObjective: Estimate the ideal wall time of a 3-stage H2D → kernel → D2H pipeline using multi-stream chunking, and identify the resource limits.

canonicalClaims.claim: Steady-state pipeline period equals the longest stage time when each pipeline stage uses an independent hardware engine (e.g., H2D copy engine, kernel engine, D2H copy engine on modern NVIDIA GPUs).
conditions: Multiple CUDA streams issued so stages can run concurrently.
Pinned host memory for full DMA bandwidth.
No cross-chunk dependencies beyond pipeline ordering.
nonImplications: Does not remove pipeline fill/drain latency; the first chunk pays full serial time.
Does not remove per-chunk resource conflicts (e.g., HBM bandwidth if kernel and copies contend).

misconceptions.claim: CUDA streams do not truly overlap H2D and D2H on the same GPU.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Modern data-center GPUs have separate H2D and D2H DMA engines; both can operate concurrently with kernel execution.
misconceptions.sourceOrEvidence: CUDA C++ Programming Guide, streams section

misconceptions.claim: N streams reduce steady-state period by 1/N.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Pipelining hides fill/drain latency, but steady-state period is set by the slowest stage; adding more streams cannot make the slowest stage faster.

misconceptions.claim: Overlap is automatic once cudaMemcpyAsync is used.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The programmer must issue kernels and copies on non-default streams and use pinned host memory; default stream serializes.

implementationFacts: Ampere and Hopper data-center GPUs typically have two DMA copy engines (one H2D, one D2H).
Pinned host memory is required for full DMA throughput and asynchronous overlap.
Default stream serializes with other streams; use explicit non-default streams for concurrency.
performanceScenarios: Data-loading pipelines for GPU training use CUDA streams to overlap H2D with GPU compute, hiding transfer time behind training kernels.
